title: Civil War Battlefields

sheetTitle.es: Campos de batalla de la Guerra Civil

summary: See how the United States split in 1861, compare the railroads of the North and the South, and find where the war's battles were fought.
subject: History
studentLogin: Not needed to explore the map

layers.name: U.S. Civil War States and Territories (1863)
layers.shows: States and territories in 1863 in five legend groups: Union free states; Union slave states (border states); slave states that seceded before Fort Sumter, April 1861; slave states that seceded after Fort Sumter; and territories. No pop-up.
layers.source: State boundaries from IPUMS NHGIS, grouped by the MapMaker team

layers.shows: The core of each battlefield, where the heaviest fighting took place. Same pop-up as the boundaries.
layers.source: National Park Service, American Battlefield Protection Program

layers.name: Boundary between Union and Confederacy

knownIssues.note: Uses the same text as the boundary layer, so it calls the core area "the battlefield area".
No pop-up is set up for the battle points in this map, so students can't click them for names and dates.

compellingQuestion.en: How did the geography of a divided nation shape the Civil War?
compellingQuestion.es: ¿Cómo influyó la geografía de una nación dividida en la Guerra Civil?

questions.task: Use the legend for U.S. Civil War States and Territories (1863) to sort the states: which seceded before Fort Sumter, which after, and which slave states stayed in the Union?

student.en: Use the legend. Which states left the Union before the attack on Fort Sumter in April 1861? Which left after? Which slave states stayed in the Union?
student.es: Usa la leyenda. ¿Qué estados dejaron la Unión antes del ataque al fuerte Sumter en abril de 1861? ¿Cuáles se fueron después? ¿Qué estados esclavistas se quedaron en la Unión?

table.caption: States by group on the map, 1863
rows: South Carolina, Mississippi, Florida, Alabama, Georgia, Louisiana, Texas
Union slave states, the border states (5)
Delaware, Maryland, Kentucky, Missouri, West Virginia
Maine, New Hampshire, Vermont, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Connecticut, New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan, Wisconsin, Minnesota, Iowa, Kansas, California, Oregon

answer.text: West Virginia split from Virginia and joined the Union as a state in June 1863, which is why it appears on this 1863 map.

questions.task: Zoom to Washington, D.C. Which states border it? Why did keeping Maryland in the Union matter?

student.en: Zoom to Washington, D.C. Which two states border it? What would have happened to the capital if Maryland had left the Union?
student.es: Acércate a Washington D. C. ¿Qué dos estados lo rodean? ¿Qué le habría pasado a la capital si Maryland hubiera dejado la Unión?

answer.text: Maryland and Virginia. Virginia joined the Confederacy, so if Maryland had seceded, the Union capital would have been surrounded by Confederate states.

questions.task: Compare the Railroads 1826 to 1863 layer (thin dark gray lines) north and south of the Boundary between Union and Confederacy (a white dashed line). Which side had more railroads, and why would that matter in a war?

student.en: Compare the railroads (thin dark gray lines) north and south of the white dashed boundary between the Union and the Confederacy. Which side had more? Why would railroads matter in a war?
student.es: Compara los ferrocarriles (líneas finas de color gris oscuro) al norte y al sur de la línea blanca discontinua que marca la frontera entre la Unión y la Confederación. ¿Qué lado tenía más? ¿Por qué importaban los ferrocarriles en una guerra?

answer.text: The North had a much denser railroad network, so it could move soldiers, food and weapons faster and farther. The map shows lines, not mileage; for figures, use the 1860 census.

questions.task: Zoom to Virginia, then to Maryland and Pennsylvania, and click the tan battlefield areas for names and sizes. Where were most battles fought, and which were fought in Union states?

student.en: Zoom to Virginia, then to Maryland and Pennsylvania. Click the tan shaded areas of two battlefields to read their names. Where were most battles fought? Name a battle fought in a Union state.
student.es: Acércate a Virginia y luego a Maryland y Pensilvania. Haz clic en las zonas color canela de dos campos de batalla para leer sus nombres. ¿Dónde se libraron la mayoría de las batallas? Nombra una batalla librada en un estado de la Unión.

answer.text: Most battlefields on the map are in the Confederate states, above all Virginia. Antietam (Maryland, 1862) and Gettysburg (Pennsylvania, 1863) were fought in Union states.

final.teacher: Students answer with evidence from at least two layers. Some ways to do it: a paragraph, a sketch of the front line with notes, or bookmarks saved for a short talk.

student.en: Answer the big question using evidence from at least two layers on the map. You can write a paragraph, sketch on the map, or both.
student.es: Responde la pregunta central con evidencia de al menos dos capas del mapa. Puedes escribir un párrafo, dibujar en el mapa o hacer ambas cosas.

beforeYouStart.en: In November 1860, Abraham Lincoln was elected president. He opposed the spread of slavery into the western territories, and Southern slave states began to leave the Union to form the Confederate States of America. In April 1861, Confederate forces attacked Fort Sumter, a Union fort in South Carolina, and the Civil War began.
beforeYouStart.es: En noviembre de 1860, Abraham Lincoln fue elegido presidente. Se oponía a que la esclavitud se extendiera a los territorios del Oeste, y los estados esclavistas del Sur comenzaron a separarse de la Unión para formar los Estados Confederados de América. En abril de 1861, fuerzas confederadas atacaron Fort Sumter, un fuerte de la Unión en Carolina del Sur, y comenzó la Guerra Civil.

readingTheMap.en: States are shaded by side in 1863: shades of blue for the Union and shades of brown for the Confederacy; the legend explains each shade. A white dashed line marks the boundary between the two sides. Thin dark gray lines are railroads built by 1863. Diamonds mark battles: blue for a Union victory, brown for a Confederate victory, white if neither side won. Bigger diamonds mean more soldiers were killed, wounded, captured or missing. Tan shaded areas show the land each battlefield covered, and areas with diagonal stripes show where the fighting was heaviest.
readingTheMap.es: Los estados aparecen sombreados según su bando en 1863: tonos azules para la Unión y tonos marrones para la Confederación; la leyenda explica cada tono. Una línea blanca discontinua marca la frontera entre los dos bandos. Las líneas finas de color gris oscuro son los ferrocarriles construidos hasta 1863. Los rombos marcan las batallas: azul si ganó la Unión, marrón si ganó la Confederación y blanco si ningún bando ganó. Los rombos más grandes indican más soldados muertos, heridos, capturados o desaparecidos. Las zonas color canela muestran el terreno que ocupó cada campo de batalla, y las zonas con rayas diagonales muestran dónde la lucha fue más intensa.

reflection.en: What did the map show you about the Civil War that you might not have noticed from reading alone?
reflection.es: ¿Qué te mostró el mapa sobre la Guerra Civil que quizá no habrías notado solo con la lectura?

teacherNotes.beforeClass: The map has no bookmarks, so students zoom to Virginia, Washington, D.C., Maryland and Pennsylvania themselves. The battle points have no pop-ups in this map; the battlefield boundary pop-ups carry the names.

misconceptions.claim: All slave states joined the Confederacy.
misconceptions.response: The legend shows five slave states that stayed in the Union: Delaware, Maryland, Kentucky, Missouri and West Virginia.

misconceptions.claim: The war was fought evenly across the North and the South.
misconceptions.response: Most battlefields on the map are in Confederate states, above all Virginia.

standards.text: Identify the division (Confederate and Union States, Border states, western territories) of the United States at the outbreak of the Civil War
Locate places and regions directly related to major eras and turning points in the United States during the 17th, 18th, and 19th centuries
Analyze the effects of physical and human geographic factors such as weather, landforms, waterways, transportation, and communication on major historical events in the United States
Use maps, satellite images, photographs, and other representations to explain relationships between the locations of places and regions, and changes in their environmental characteristics
Explain multiple causes and effects of events and developments in the past

keyFacts: Seceded before Fort Sumter (April 1861), per the map: South Carolina, Mississippi, Florida, Alabama, Georgia, Louisiana and Texas.
Seceded after Fort Sumter, per the map: Virginia, Arkansas, North Carolina and Tennessee.
Union slave (border) states on the 1863 map: Delaware, Maryland, Kentucky, Missouri and West Virginia (a state from June 1863).
Antietam (Maryland, 1862) and Gettysburg (Pennsylvania, 1863) were fought in Union states.
